title: Insertion Sort List
description: Brute force to optimized: an array-based insertion sort versus a direct linked-list adaptation that reuses existing nodes.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list, sort the list using INSERTION SORT, and return the sorted list's head.

blocks.caption: Each node from the unsorted portion is taken one at a time and inserted directly into its correct position within the growing sorted portion

blocks.text: Insertion sort works by maintaining a growing SORTED portion; each new element from the unsorted portion is inserted directly into its correct position within that sorted portion, one element at a time.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting a Hand of Playing Cards
blocks.text: Exactly like sorting a hand of playing cards as they are dealt to you, one at a time: each new card is slid into its correct position among the cards ALREADY sorted in your hand, shifting nothing else out of place. By the time every card has been placed, the entire hand is sorted, without ever needing to look at all the cards at once.

blocks.text: Since the specific algorithm is named directly in the problem, the main task is adapting the classic insertion sort mechanics (grow a sorted portion, insert each new element into its correct spot) onto a linked list's node re-linking operations.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A separate "sorted result" list needs to be built up, anchored by a dummy head, since the final sorted head might end up being a completely different node than the original head.

Observation 2: For each node taken from the (still linked, original-order) unsorted portion, a walk through the CURRENT sorted result is needed to find exactly where it belongs (the first position whose value is not smaller than it).

Observation 3: Crucially, before re-linking the current node into the sorted result, its ORIGINAL next pointer (into the remaining unsorted portion) must be saved, since that pointer is about to be overwritten by the insertion itself.

Observation 4: Once inserted, continue processing the unsorted portion using that SAVED next pointer, not whatever the just-inserted node's next now points to (which is now part of the sorted result).

Recognizing that "save next before re-linking" is essential here, exactly as in other in-place linked-list transformations, avoids losing track of the remaining unsorted portion.

This is a direct linked-list adaptation of the classic insertion sort algorithm: a growing sorted result, with each new node inserted into its correct position by walking from the sorted result's dummy head.
Extract every value into an array, then perform a standard array-based insertion sort, shifting elements as needed to make room for each newly inserted value.

items: Walk through the list, collecting every value into an array.
For each value, walk backward through the already-sorted prefix of the result, shifting larger values right, and insert the current value into its correct spot.

codes.python:
def insertion_sort_list(values):
    result = []
    for v in values:                                                       # take each value one at a time, exactly like card-sorting by hand
        i = len(result)
        while i > 0 and result[i - 1] > v:                                 # shift larger values right to make room
            i -= 1
        result.insert(i, v)
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(insertion_sort_list([4, 2, 1, 3]))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: This directly implements the classic array-based insertion sort algorithm, matching the problem's explicit naming of the required technique.
Working on a plain array sidesteps the linked-list-specific bookkeeping (saving the original next pointer) that the true linked-list version requires.

blocks.text: Correctly sorts the values using the specified algorithm, though it does not directly produce the required re-linked linked-list structure.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case (a descending input), matching insertion sort's known complexity.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array.

Limitation: extracting into an array does not produce the actual required linked-list structure; performing the insertion sort directly on the linked list's own nodes achieves the same result while reusing the existing nodes.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force sorts a separate array, not the actual linked list. Instead, build a sorted RESULT list (with a dummy head) directly from the original nodes. For each node taken from the unsorted portion (in its original order), save its next pointer, then walk the sorted result to find its correct insertion point, and re-link it there. Continue with the saved next pointer.

Initialize a dummy head for the sorted result. Walk curr through the original list: save next = curr.next; walk prev from the dummy head while prev.next exists and prev.next.val < curr.val; insert curr right after prev (curr.next = prev.next, prev.next = curr); continue with curr = next.
Build a sorted result list directly, walking it once per node from the unsorted portion to find each node's correct insertion point.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The fully built sorted result is [1,2,3,4], matching the expected output.

codes.python:
def insertion_sort_list(head):
    dummy = ListNode(0)                                                     # sorted result begins empty, anchored by a dummy head
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next                                              # save curr's original next BEFORE it gets re-linked
        prev = dummy
        while prev.next and prev.next.val < curr.val:                       # walk the sorted portion to find curr's correct spot
            prev = prev.next
        curr.next = prev.next                                               # insert curr right there
        prev.next = curr
        curr = next_node                                                    # continue with the ORIGINAL next node from the unsorted portion
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(4, ListNode(2, ListNode(1, ListNode(3))))
    result = insertion_sort_list(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case, matching classic insertion sort (each of the n insertions can require walking through up to n already-sorted nodes).
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes.

At every point during the process, the "sorted result" list is genuinely fully sorted, by insertion sort's core invariant: each new node is placed at the first position where it is not greater than what follows, which correctly maintains sortedness after every single insertion. Saving curr's original next pointer BEFORE the insertion is what allows the remaining unsorted portion to still be correctly walked afterward, since curr's own next pointer gets overwritten as part of the insertion itself.

items: The dummy head for the SORTED RESULT is separate and distinct from the original list being consumed, which is walked via curr.
Saving next = curr.next before any re-linking is the critical detail that prevents losing track of the remaining unsorted portion.
The inner while loop's condition (prev.next.val < curr.val, using strict less-than) ensures equal values are inserted AFTER existing equal values, keeping the sort stable.

blocks.text: Insertion sort directly translates onto a linked list by maintaining a separate sorted result (with a dummy head) and inserting each node from the unsorted portion into its correct spot, carefully saving each node's original next pointer before it gets overwritten by the insertion.

items: Forgetting to save curr's original next pointer before re-linking it into the sorted result, permanently losing track of the remaining unsorted nodes.
Using a single shared list instead of a genuinely SEPARATE sorted result, causing confusion about which portion is sorted and which is not.
Using a non-strict comparison (<=) in the insertion walk, which would break stability by inserting equal values BEFORE existing equal ones instead of after.

items: Explicitly acknowledging insertion sort's O(n^2) worst-case time (rather than claiming this achieves the same efficiency as merge sort) demonstrates honest complexity awareness, since the problem specifically asks for THIS algorithm despite it being asymptotically slower.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Sort using INSERTION SORT specifically" (as opposed to "sort efficiently") points toward directly simulating the classic insertion sort mechanics, not substituting a faster algorithm like merge sort.

items: Why not use merge sort here instead, since it is asymptotically faster? The problem specifically names insertion sort as the required algorithm; Sort List (elsewhere in this category) is the appropriate place for the more efficient merge sort approach.

What is the best-case time complexity, and when does it occur? O(n), when the input is already sorted, since each node is inserted immediately at the sorted result's current tail without any backward walking.

How would you make this insertion sort stable (preserving the relative order of equal values)? Using a strict less-than comparison (prev.next.val < curr.val, not <=) in the insertion walk, exactly as implemented, already achieves this.

A direct, algorithm-specific counterpart to Sort List (which uses the more efficient merge sort) elsewhere in this category, both building a result via re-linking existing nodes rather than creating new ones.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (linked-list insertion sort): O(n^2) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Linked-list insertion sort (growing a sorted result, inserting each node into its correct spot)

Core Idea: Maintain a separate sorted result list with a dummy head; for each node from the unsorted portion, save its original next pointer, then walk the sorted result to find and perform its correct insertion
Time: O(n^2) worst case
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: The node's original next pointer must be saved BEFORE it gets overwritten by the insertion, or the remaining unsorted portion is lost
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Save next, walk the sorted result to find curr's spot, insert it there, continue with the saved next
